Ecology, Ecosystems and Energy Flow
The base of every environment question

Ecology appears in UPSC Prelims almost every year. Questions on food chains, pyramids, keystone species and biomagnification are routine. GS Paper III also uses these ideas. Pollution, climate and biodiversity answers all rest on how an ecosystem works. If energy flow is clear, much of the syllabus becomes easy.
What ecology studies

Ecology is the study of how organisms relate to each other and to their surroundings. The word was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866. The term ecosystem was coined by A.G. Tansley in 1935. The levels run from organism to population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere. An ecosystem has abiotic parts (light, soil, water) and biotic parts: producers , consumers and decomposers .
Grazing, detritus and the web

A grazing food chain starts with green plants and moves to herbivores and carnivores. A detritus food chain starts with dead matter, eaten by earthworms and fungi. On land, much more energy flows through the detritus chain. Each feeding level is a trophic level . Real ecosystems form a food web with many linked chains. A web is more stable because an animal can switch food if one source fails.
The ten percent law

Sunlight is the only input. Producers capture only a small part of it. Raymond Lindeman (1942) showed that about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost as heat in respiration. So energy flow is one-way . Nutrients cycle, but energy does not. This is also why food chains rarely have more than four or five links.
GPP, NPP and who is most productive

Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total energy fixed by producers. Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the energy used by plants in respiration. NPP is the food available to consumers. Per unit area, estuaries, coral reefs and tropical rainforests are among the most productive. Open oceans are poor per area but huge in total because they cover so much of Earth.
Numbers, biomass and energy

The pyramid of energy is always upright. Energy cannot increase going up. The pyramid of biomass is inverted in the sea. Tiny phytoplankton have a small standing crop but multiply fast, and they feed a larger mass of zooplankton and fish. The pyramid of numbers can be inverted too: one big tree supports thousands of insects.
Poisons climb the chain

Some substances are not broken down or excreted: DDT, mercury, cadmium. They build up in fat or tissue. This is bioaccumulation . When the concentration rises at each higher trophic level, it is biomagnification . Top predators suffer most. DDT thinned the eggshells of eagles and falcons. Mercury caused Minamata disease in Japan (1956). Cadmium caused Itai-itai disease.
Niche, keystone species and ecotone

Habitat is where an organism lives. Niche is its role: what it eats, where it lives and how it behaves. A keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers. Robert Paine (1966) showed this with the starfish Pisaster on rocky shores. An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems, such as mangroves between land and sea. It often holds more species. This is the edge effect .
Vultures and the ecosystem service

India’s vultures crashed by over 95 percent in the 1990s. The cause was diclofenac , a painkiller given to cattle. Vultures ate the carcasses and died of kidney failure. Without vultures, carcasses rotted, stray dogs increased and rabies risk rose. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. This is a clean example of how one lost scavenger breaks the detritus link. The Sundarbans, Western Ghats and Chilika are all good examples of linked food webs under stress.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Ecosystem services are the lifeline of human welfare. Discuss with Indian examples.” Structure: define services (provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting); give Indian cases (mangroves as storm buffers, wetlands as flood sponges, pollinators); name the threat; end with policy (PES, Green Credit). Mains-style: “Why is biomagnification a concern for human health?” Define, give DDT and mercury, link to Indian pesticide use, suggest bans and organic methods. Prelims tip: Energy pyramids are always upright. Biomass pyramids can be inverted only in aquatic systems. Learn who coined each term.
Biogeochemical Cycles and Ecological Succession
Nutrients cycle, energy does not

Plants and animals use the same atoms again and again. These loops are the biogeochemical cycles . UPSC asks about them in Prelims, and they explain pollution problems such as eutrophication, acid rain and fertiliser overuse. Succession explains how bare land turns into forest and why a disturbed ecosystem recovers. Both topics are short, but they carry sure marks.
Gaseous and sedimentary cycles

In a gaseous cycle the main reservoir is the atmosphere or ocean. Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles are gaseous. In a sedimentary cycle the reservoir is the Earth’s crust. Phosphorus and sulphur are sedimentary (sulphur has a small gas phase). Cycles move through pools (reservoirs) and fluxes (flows). Humans now change the flows more than nature does.
Fast and slow loops

Plants take in CO2 by photosynthesis. Respiration, decomposition and burning return it. The biggest store is the rocks (limestone and fossil fuels) . Among active stores, the ocean is the largest. Burning fossil fuels moves ancient carbon into the air in a few centuries. That is why CO2 has gone past 420 ppm (as of 2025) from about 280 ppm before industry.
Why free nitrogen is useless to plants

Air is about 78 percent nitrogen, but plants cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation converts it. Bacteria such as Rhizobium (in legume roots), Azotobacter and cyanobacteria like Nostoc do this. Lightning also fixes some. Then ammonification makes ammonia from dead matter. Nitrification turns it into nitrite ( Nitrosomonas ) and nitrate ( Nitrobacter ). Denitrification ( Pseudomonas ) returns nitrogen gas to air.
Rock cycles

Phosphorus comes from rock weathering. It has no gas phase. It is often the limiting nutrient in fresh water. Excess phosphate from detergents and fertiliser causes eutrophication : algal bloom, oxygen loss, fish kills. Sulphur enters the air as SO2 from volcanoes and burning coal. It becomes sulphuric acid in acid rain . Plankton also release dimethyl sulphide, which helps form clouds.
From bare rock to forest

Succession is the orderly change of a community over time. Primary succession starts on bare ground with no soil: new lava, rock or a retreating glacier. Pioneers such as lichens come first (a lithosere ). On open water it is a hydrosere . Secondary succession starts where soil survives: after a fire, flood or abandoned farm. It is much faster.
Seral stages

The steps are called seral stages . The final stable community is the climax community . Early on, production exceeds respiration; at climax they roughly balance. Autogenic succession is driven by the community itself. Allogenic succession is driven by outside forces such as climate. Species diversity and soil depth rise with time.
Is there one climax?

Clements (early 20th century) argued for a single climate climax in a region (monoclimax). Later ecologists such as Gleason and Tansley stressed that local soil and chance matter, so many end states are possible. Modern thinking sees ecosystems as shifting, not fixed. This matters for restoration policy: you cannot simply plant any tree and expect the old forest.
Fertiliser, soil and recovery

Over-use of urea has unbalanced India’s nitrogen cycle. The government pushed neem-coated urea (2015), the Soil Health Card (2015) and nano urea to cut waste. Run-off nitrate and phosphate cause algal blooms in lakes. Secondary succession is the basis of natural regeneration in jhum fallows of the North-East and in mine land reclamation. Mangrove colonisation in the Sundarbans is a classic example of succession in a delta.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Discuss the impact of excessive fertiliser use on the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles in India.” Structure: explain both cycles briefly; show the imbalance (eutrophication, groundwater nitrate, N2O emissions); give policy (neem-coated urea, nano urea, soil health card, organic farming). Mains-style: “Distinguish primary and secondary succession with examples.” Prelims tip: Phosphorus has no gaseous phase. Denitrification returns N2 to air. Succession on rock is a lithosere; on water, a hydrosere.
Terrestrial and Aquatic Ecosystems
Biomes and ecosystems link to the map

Prelims often asks you to match a biome with a climate, a plant or an animal. Mains asks about forests, wetlands and coastal systems. This lesson gives the skeleton. Know the main biomes, India’s forest types, forest cover numbers and the zones of lakes and oceans.
A biome is a large ecosystem type

A biome is a major community shaped by climate, mainly temperature and rainfall. The main ones are tundra, taiga (boreal forest), temperate deciduous forest, grassland, savanna, tropical rainforest, desert and Mediterranean scrub. An ecosystem is smaller and can be a pond or a patch of forest. Biomes change with latitude and with altitude.
Quick guide

Tundra: very cold, permafrost, mosses and lichens, reindeer. Taiga: conifers, long winters; the largest land biome by area. Temperate grassland: prairies (N. America), steppes (Eurasia), pampas (Argentina), veldt (S. Africa), downs (Australia). Savanna: grass with scattered trees; Africa’s plains. Tropical rainforest: hot, wet, richest biodiversity. Desert: under 25 cm rain; succulents like cacti.
Types and cover

Champion and Seth (1968) classified India’s forests into 16 major types, with tropical moist deciduous as the largest group in area. As of ISFR 2023 (the latest I could confirm), India’s forest cover is about 21.76 percent of the area and tree cover about 3.41 percent. Total green cover is about 25.17 percent. The India State of Forest Report is released by the Forest Survey of India every two years.
Where the forests are

By area, Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover, then Arunachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. By percentage of its area, Mizoram, Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar rank highest. The National Forest Policy 1988 aims for one-third of land under forest or tree cover, and two-thirds in hills. India is still below that.
Still and flowing water

Lentic means still water: lakes, ponds. Lotic means flowing water: rivers, streams. A deep lake has three zones. The littoral zone is the shallow edge with rooted plants. The limnetic zone is open water where light reaches. The profundal zone is deep and dark. Lakes age through eutrophication and silting.
Ocean zones

The sea has a lighted photic zone and a dark aphotic zone . The neritic zone is over the continental shelf and holds most fish. Pelagic means open water; benthic means the sea floor. An estuary is where a river meets the sea. Salinity varies and nutrients are rich, so it is a nursery for fish and prawns. Upwelling brings nutrients to the surface and creates rich fisheries, as off Peru.
Forest cover is not forest quality

India’s cover has risen on paper, but experts point out that the count includes plantations, orchards and bamboo. Natural forest and old-growth stands may be shrinking, and open forest is increasing while very dense forest changes slowly. The question is whether we protect ecosystem function or just green area. This is a standard Mains argument.
Special systems

Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating phumdis . Keibul Lamjao is the only floating national park in the world and shelters the sangai (brow-antlered deer). Chilika is Asia’s largest brackish water lagoon. The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove delta. The Western Ghats and Eastern Himalaya are montane forest hotspots. The Thar and Ladakh cold desert are the dry biomes.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is the difference between forest cover and tree cover? Why is India’s quality of forest a concern?” Structure: definitions (ISFR terms); latest numbers (as of ISFR 2023); concerns (plantations counted, loss of natural forest, diversion for projects); remedies (CAMPA, community management). Prelims tip: Pampas is Argentina, veldt is South Africa, steppe is Eurasia. Loktak’s phumdis are floating biomass. Champion and Seth gave 16 types.
Biodiversity: Levels, Hotspots and Threats
Biodiversity is asked every year

Hotspots, endemic species, invasive plants and the global biodiversity framework come up often in Prelims. Mains uses them in questions on conservation, climate and development. India holds about 2.4 percent of Earth’s land and a much larger share (roughly 7 to 8 percent) of known species. It is one of the megadiverse countries.
Three levels

Genetic diversity : variation within a species, such as thousands of rice varieties. Species diversity : the number and spread of species. Ecosystem diversity : variety of habitats like forests, wetlands and deserts. Whittaker split species diversity into alpha (within a habitat), beta (between habitats) and gamma (across a region).
Where is diversity high?

Diversity rises toward the equator. This is the latitudinal gradient : tropical regions have more stable climate, more energy and a longer evolutionary history. The species-area relationship (Humboldt) says larger areas hold more species. The equation S = CA^Z gives a slope (Z) of about 0.1 to 0.2 on regional scales. This is why habitat fragmentation matters.
The idea

Norman Myers (1988) proposed biodiversity hotspots. Conservation International now uses two tests: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and at least 70 percent of original habitat lost . There are about 36 hotspots worldwide. They cover a small fraction of land but hold a very large share of endemic plants and vertebrates.
Where they are

Himalaya : the whole range, including Bhutan, Nepal and parts of Tibet. Indo-Burma : North-East India south of the Brahmaputra, plus Myanmar and more. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka : very high endemism. Sundaland : in India, only the Nicobar Islands. Hotspots are defined by Norman Myers' criteria: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70 percent of original habitat. The Eastern Himalaya part is rich in orchids and rhododendrons, and the Western Ghats hold many amphibians. India's Indo-Burma portion includes Manipur, Mizoram and Nagaland, and the Nicobar Islands form its Sundaland part.
Why species are lost

Jared Diamond called the main causes the “evil quartet”: habitat loss and fragmentation , overexploitation , alien species invasion and co-extinction . Climate change and pollution are now added. Habitat loss is the top cause. Poaching, the wildlife trade and human-animal conflict add pressure. Habitat loss includes clearing for farms, mines, dams and roads, and also fragmentation, which splits a large habitat into patches too small for wide-ranging animals such as elephants and tigers. Edge effects then make the remaining patches poorer. Co-extinction means a species dies because its partner does, such as a parasite that depends on one host. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) also named climate change, pollution and overexploitation among the main drivers.
Plants that take over

India’s major invasives include Lantana camara , water hyacinth , Prosopis juliflora , Parthenium and Chromolaena . They crowd out native plants and reduce grazing and water. The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 gave the Centre power to regulate invasive alien species. Control costs are high, and removal programmes in tiger reserves such as Bandipur and Mudumalai are ongoing. Invasives spread through trade, travel and deliberate introduction. Water hyacinth, native to South America, was brought as an ornamental plant and now chokes ponds and lakes, cutting oxygen for fish. Lantana came from tropical America in the colonial period as a garden shrub and now covers large forest areas. Alien species often lack natural predators in the new home, which is why they spread fast. The Convention on Biological Diversity (Article 8h) asks countries to prevent and control them.
Kunming-Montreal, 2022

The Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio, 1992) set the base. In December 2022 at COP15 (Montreal) , nations adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with 23 targets for 2030. Key targets: protect 30 percent of land and sea by 2030 (“30 by 30”), restore 30 percent of degraded areas, and mobilise about $200 billion a year from all sources. Developed countries are to give $20 billion a year in international finance by 2025 and $30 billion by 2030.
Law and plans

The Biological Diversity Act 2002 set up the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai, 2003), State Biodiversity Boards and local Biodiversity Management Committees . It covers access and benefit sharing, based on the Nagoya Protocol. The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 eased rules for AYUSH users and decriminalised some offences. India released an updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan with national targets in line with the Kunming-Montreal framework (as of 2024). CBD COP17 was due in Armenia in late 2026; check its outcome before the exam.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What are biodiversity hotspots? Why is the Western Ghats a hotspot, and what threatens it?” Structure: definition and two criteria; Western Ghats endemism; threats (mining, plantations, tourism, landslides); Gadgil and Kasturirangan reports; remedies. Mains-style: “Invasive alien species are a silent threat to Indian ecosystems. Discuss.” Prelims tip: Remember the two hotspot criteria numbers (1,500 and 70 percent). India’s hotspot in the Nicobar Islands belongs to Sundaland.
In-situ and Ex-situ Conservation: Protected Areas
Prelims favourite

Questions on national parks, biosphere reserves, tiger reserves and World Heritage Sites come almost every year. Mains asks about conflict between people and protected areas. The key is to know which law creates which category. A simple way to remember is by layers: legal categories under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, then UNESCO designations such as biosphere reserves and World Heritage Sites, then ex-situ centres. Conflict questions often involve relocation of villages, forest rights under the 2006 Act, and human-elephant or human-tiger conflict near reserve borders.
In-situ and ex-situ

In-situ conservation protects species in their natural home. Examples: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves. Ex-situ conservation protects them outside: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation. In-situ is better for whole ecosystems. Ex-situ is a backup for species on the edge. Examples of ex-situ work include zoos regulated by the Central Zoo Authority, botanical gardens, and the National Gene Bank run by NBPGR in New Delhi. A key tool is captive breeding followed by reintroduction, as with the gharial. In-situ keeps evolution going in the wild, which ex-situ cannot copy. Most experts say the two approaches work best together, with in-situ as the main strategy.
Under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972

National Park : Section 35. Strictest. No grazing or private rights. Wildlife Sanctuary : Section 26A. Some human activity may be allowed. Conservation Reserve (Section 36A) and Community Reserve (Section 36C): added by the 2002 amendment on government land and community/private land. Tiger Reserve : Section 38V, managed by the National Tiger Conservation Authority. The key difference is that in a sanctuary some activities such as grazing may be permitted by the Chief Wildlife Warden, while in a national park none is allowed. Both are notified by the State government. The 2002 amendment added Conservation and Community Reserves so that people's land could be protected without taking away their rights. Tiger reserves have a core (critical tiger habitat) and a buffer where people and wildlife coexist.
Not under the Wildlife Act

The idea comes from UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere (MAB) programme (1971). India has a national scheme from 1986 and has about 18 reserves. Each reserve has a core zone (strictly protected), a buffer zone (limited use) and a transition zone (people live and farm). Nilgiri (1986) was first. UNESCO recognises 13 Indian reserves (Cold Desert added in 2025) in the world network, including Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar and Khangchendzonga.
How much is protected

As of recent MoEFCC figures, India has over 1,000 protected areas, roughly 100 national parks and over 500 sanctuaries. They cover about 5 percent of India’s land (figures change slightly each year). The target of 30 by 30 includes OECMs : other effective area-based measures such as community-run sites that are not formally protected.
Natural sites in India

India’s natural World Heritage Sites include Kaziranga , Manas , Keoladeo , Sundarbans , Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers , Western Ghats and Great Himalayan National Park . Khangchendzonga is a mixed site. World Heritage status comes from the 1972 UNESCO convention and listing does not by itself change Indian law.
Zoos and gene banks

The Central Zoo Authority (1992) regulates zoos. The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in Delhi runs the national seed gene bank. The National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources at Karnal holds animal genetic material. Conservation breeding is used for the Great Indian Bustard (a centre at Jaisalmer), the gharial and vultures. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway is the world’s backup.
Fortress conservation or people’s rights?

Critics say removing people from parks creates displacement and hostility. Supporters say core areas need inviolate space for large predators. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises rights and allows Critical Wildlife Habitats . Sacred groves (Meghalaya’s Law Kyntang, Rajasthan’s Orans, Kerala’s Kavu) show that community conservation also works.
Examples to remember

Kaziranga protects the one-horned rhino. Gir holds the Asiatic lion. Keoladeo is a Ramsar and World Heritage bird site. Simlipal and Nilgiri are biosphere reserves. Sundarbans is both a tiger reserve and biosphere reserve. Eco-sensitive zones (ESZ) around parks regulate activity in a buffer, usually up to 10 km unless fixed otherwise.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Distinguish between in-situ and ex-situ conservation. Which is better for India’s biodiversity?” Structure: definitions; examples; strengths and limits of each; they are complementary; policy (CAMPA, community reserves). Mains-style: “Protected areas versus people: how can both be served?” Prelims tip: Biosphere reserves are not under the WPA. Community reserves are on private or community land. National parks allow no grazing.
Species in News and the IUCN Red List
Species in news is a Prelims staple

Almost every Prelims paper has a question on a species: its status, habitat or the park where it lives. UPSC picks animals that were in the news. The method is simple: learn the IUCN status, the Schedule and the place. This lesson gives the system and the animals that recur most.
What the IUCN is

The International Union for Conservation of Nature was founded in 1948 and is based in Gland, Switzerland. It is a union of states and NGOs. Its Red List of Threatened Species is the main global record of extinction risk. The Red List is a scientific assessment, not a law. It does not protect a species by itself. Indian protection comes from the Wildlife (Protection) Act and CITES.
The ladder of risk

From worst to best: Extinct (EX) , Extinct in the Wild (EW) , Critically Endangered (CR) , Endangered (EN) , Vulnerable (VU) , Near Threatened (NT) , Least Concern (LC) . Two more: Data Deficient (DD) and Not Evaluated (NE) . Threatened means CR, EN and VU together. Criteria use population decline, range size, population size and extinction probability.
The Red List in 2026

The Red List now covers well over 170,000 species, and roughly 28 percent of those assessed are threatened. The October 2025 update listed about 172,600 species assessed, of which about 48,600 (around 28%) are threatened. Positive news exists. In October 2025 the green turtle was moved from Endangered to Least Concern globally after conservation gains.
Status of Indian flagships

Tiger : Endangered. Asiatic lion : Endangered. Asian elephant : Endangered. Indian rhino : Vulnerable. Snow leopard : Vulnerable. Cheetah : Vulnerable globally. Ganges river dolphin : Endangered. The IUCN Red List is revised through the year, so these statuses can change. The snow leopard was moved from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2017. The Asiatic lion lives only in Gir and its surroundings in Gujarat. The Ganges river dolphin is India's National Aquatic Animal, and the Indian rhino is found mainly in Assam.
The critically endangered list

Great Indian Bustard : Critically Endangered, mainly Rajasthan. Gharial : Critically Endangered, mainly in the Chambal. Pygmy hog : Critically Endangered, Assam. White-rumped, Indian and slender-billed vultures : Critically Endangered. Hangul (Kashmir stag): Critically Endangered, Dachigam. Sangai (brow-antlered deer) is Endangered. A species' status changes with new assessments, so always check the latest IUCN list. Vultures collapsed in the 1990s after cattle were treated with the drug diclofenac, which poisoned birds that fed on carcasses; the veterinary use was banned in 2006. The Great Indian Bustard faces deaths from collisions with power lines. The pygmy hog is bred in captivity at Basistha near Guwahati and released in Assam grasslands.
International trade and migration

CITES (1973, in force 1975) regulates trade. Appendix I bans commercial trade in species threatened with extinction. Appendix II allows controlled trade. Appendix III lists species a country asks others to help protect. CMS (Bonn, 1979) protects migratory species. India hosted CMS COP13 at Gandhinagar in February 2020 (Great Indian Bustard was a theme). The Wildlife Act 2022 now has a schedule for CITES specimens. CITES works through permits: exporting a listed specimen needs a permit from the exporting country's authority. India has been a party since 1976. Under CMS, Appendix I lists migratory species in danger, while Appendix II lists those that need international agreements. Regional agreements and MoUs, such as the Siberian Crane MoU, follow from it. India has been a CMS party since 1983.
Flagships versus the quiet species

Charismatic animals attract funds: tigers, lions, elephants. Plants, insects and amphibians are far more threatened but get little attention. Critics also say the Red List status is global. A species may be Least Concern globally yet be rare in India. Local lists and the national Schedules therefore matter.
How news links to learning

When a species is in the news, ask five things: Red List status, Wildlife Act Schedule, habitat state, threat, and any project (Project Tiger, Project Cheetah, Project Dolphin, Great Indian Bustard recovery). India’s Wildlife Act Schedule I gives the highest protection; the 2022 amendment kept it for the most endangered. The Great Indian Bustard also gained attention in a 2021 Supreme Court case on power lines in its habitat.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is the role of the IUCN Red List in conservation planning? Mention its limits.” Structure: purpose; categories; how India uses it; limits (global scale, data gaps, not legally binding); conclusion. Mains-style: “Why do species like the Great Indian Bustard survive in the face of development pressure?” Prelims tip: Learn the “CR list”: GIB, gharial, pygmy hog, hangul, three vultures. Remember threatened = CR + EN + VU.
Wildlife Laws and Projects in India
Law plus projects equals half the topic

UPSC asks both: what the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 does, and what each project achieved. Cheetah, tiger, elephant and dolphin projects are in the news every year. This lesson also uses current facts. Numbers change, so the year is marked. Expect the Act in Prelims through its sections, schedules and bodies, and the projects in Mains through a success versus gaps argument. Project Tiger began in 1973, Project Elephant in 1992, and the Gangetic dolphin received a project in later years. Remember to link each project with the nodal agency and the law that gives it legal force.
Core features

The Act came after the 1972 Stockholm conference. It bans hunting (Section 9), creates protected areas, sets up Wildlife Advisory Boards, and gives schedules of protected species. Penalties are in Section 51. India adopted a Constitutional base in 1976 (42nd Amendment): forests and wild animals moved to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A and 17B), and Article 48A and 51A(g) were added. The Act created schedules of species. Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II carry the highest protection and heaviest penalties. After the 2022 amendment the Act has four schedules, with a new one for CITES-listed specimens, and the old vermin schedule was dropped. The Chief Wildlife Warden is the key State official. The National Board for Wildlife, chaired by the Prime Minister, advises the Centre.
What changed (in force 2023)

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 did these things: it cut the schedules from six to four; it dropped the vermin schedule; it added a schedule for CITES specimens and made the Centre the CITES authority; it gave power to regulate invasive alien species ; and it allowed states to reconstitute their Wildlife Advisory Board as a Standing Committee. It also allows voluntary surrender of captive wild animals and regulates elephant transfer for religious uses.
Gaps and concerns

Critics say the Amendment shifts power to the Centre and weakens oversight of captive elephants. Supporters say it brings India in line with CITES and helps curb invasives. Enforcement is weaker than the law. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007) tackles trade, but conviction rates are low.
The model

Project Tiger began in 1973 (Corbett was first). The National Tiger Conservation Authority became statutory in 2006. The 2022 estimate reported at least 3,167 tigers from camera traps and a mean estimate near 3,682 , which is about 70 percent of the world’s wild tigers. The next estimation (sixth cycle) began in 2025–26 and its report is expected in 2027. India has 58 tiger reserves in 18 states (as of 2026).
As of 2026

The cheetah went extinct in India in 1952. Eight Namibian cheetahs were released at Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh) on 17 September 2022. Twelve more came from South Africa in 2023. Cubs are now born in India. As of September 2026, secondary reports count about 52 cheetahs , including around 32 born in India, with a few at Gandhi Sagar sanctuary. Banni (Gujarat) and other sites are being prepared. Botswana is a new source country.
Quick table

Project Elephant (1992): corridors and elephant reserves. The 2017 census counted 27,312 elephants. The DNA-based 2021–25 estimate, released in October 2025, counted about 22,446 elephants; it uses a new method, so it is not directly comparable. Project Snow Leopard (2009) and the SECURE Himalaya programme. Project Dolphin (announced 2020) for river and ocean dolphins. Crocodile Conservation Project (1975) and gharial work in the Chambal. Project Lion for Gujarat’s Asiatic lions; the 16th lion census (May 2025) counted 891, up from 674 in 2020.
Is translocation worth it?

Cheetah supporters say it restores a grassland predator and funds grasslands. Critics say India lacks enough open space, deaths were high in early years, and money would be better spent on the Great Indian Bustard or caracal. The Supreme Court monitored the project and asked for more sites. The same question applies to tiger relocation: how many animals can the land hold?
Related laws

Related laws: Forest Conservation Act 1980 (now renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam after the 2023 amendment), Forest Rights Act 2006 , Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Environment Protection Act 1986 . The Supreme Court’s M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024) case, on the Great Indian Bustard, recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Evaluate the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022. Does it strengthen conservation?” Structure: key changes; positives (CITES, invasives, rationalised schedules); negatives (centralisation, captive animals, enforcement); way forward. Mains-style: “Project Cheetah: success or experiment? Discuss.” Prelims tip: The 2022 Act cut schedules from six to four. Kuno is in Madhya Pradesh. NTCA is statutory since 2006.
Air Pollution and Air Quality
Winter smog is a yearly headline

Every winter Delhi and the Indo-Gangetic Plain choke on smog. UPSC asks about the Air Act, AQI, NCAP, BS-VI, stubble burning and health. Mains wants causes, policy and a way forward. The numbers below matter in Prelims. The causes and policy gaps matter in Mains.
Primary and secondary pollutants

Primary pollutants are released directly: SO2, NOx, CO, particles. Secondary pollutants form in the air: ground-level ozone and PAN. PM2.5 and PM10 are particles under 2.5 and 10 micrometres. PM2.5 enters the lungs and blood and causes the most harm. Other pollutants: lead, ammonia, benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic, nickel.
Two kinds

Photochemical smog (Los Angeles type) needs sunlight, NOx and volatile organic compounds. It makes ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN). Classical or sulphurous smog (London 1952) comes from coal smoke and SO2 in cold, humid air. The Great Smog of 1952 led to the UK Clean Air Act 1956. Delhi’s winter smog combines both with temperature inversion.
NAAQS and AQI

India’s National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009) cover 12 pollutants. The annual limit for PM2.5 is 40 µg/m3 and the 24-hour limit is 60. For PM10 they are 60 and 100. The National Air Quality Index was launched in 2014 with six bands: Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor and Severe. The WHO guideline (2021) is much tighter: 5 µg/m3 annual for PM2.5.
Air Act 1981 and the rest

The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 follows the Stockholm conference. It set up the CPCB and State Boards and allowed air pollution control areas. The Environment Protection Act 1986 provides the umbrella rules. For Delhi NCR, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) was set up in 2020 and given statutory form in 2021. The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) imposes steps as AQI worsens.
Policy tools

The National Clean Air Programme (January 2019) targets about 130 non-attainment cities. It began with a 20 to 30 percent cut in PM goal by 2024 against 2017, later revised to 40 percent by 2025–26. Money flows through the PRANA portal and the 15th Finance Commission’s performance grants. Bharat Stage VI fuel and engine norms started in April 2020, skipping BS-V. Other steps: Ujjwala LPG, power plant FGD rules, EV push (PM E-DRIVE), and subsidies for crop residue machines.
Who pollutes

Main sources are vehicles, road dust, construction, coal power plants, industry, biomass cooking and crop-residue burning in Punjab and Haryana in October-November. Studies differ on shares because meteorology varies. Transport and dust dominate in Delhi on most days; stubble contributes a large spike in some weeks. Indoor air from solid-fuel cooking remains a major rural killer.
Quick fixes or deep fixes?

Odd-even schemes, smog towers and cloud seeding trials give visible action but little evidence of big impact. Critics say the airshed approach across states is the real need, with enforcement on industry, transport and power. Another debate: tighten standards to WHO levels or make them achievable first? A third: is air quality a health emergency or a development trade-off?
Beyond Delhi

Many studies rank cities in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and parts of the North-East among the most polluted in the world. The health burden includes asthma, COPD and early deaths. The Sustainable Development Goals and the Right to Life (Article 21) frame clean air as a right. Courts have repeatedly directed Delhi on vehicles, fuel and construction dust (M.C. Mehta cases).
How to answer

Mains-style: “Why does northern India suffer from severe air pollution every winter? Suggest measures.” Structure: causes (inversion, stubble, vehicles, dust); health and economic cost; current measures (NCAP, GRAP, CAQM, BS-VI); gaps; airshed approach, crop diversification, public transport. Prelims tip: Learn six AQI bands, the NAAQS year (2009), NCAP (2019) and BS-VI (2020). Air Act is 1981; Water Act is 1974.
Water, Soil and Noise Pollution
Everyday pollution, regular questions

Rivers, groundwater and noise are classic GS-III topics. Prelims tests terms like BOD and COD. Mains asks for causes, laws and schemes like Namami Gange. One idea ties everything: pollution is not only about industry. Sewage and farming matter most in India. Water, soil and noise pollution are linked: fertilisers and pesticides from soil wash into rivers, and untreated sewage reaches groundwater. Also remember that rural India faces chemical contamination of groundwater, while cities face sewage and traffic noise. Link each type to its law and its monitoring agency, and always add a named scheme.
Indicators

Dissolved oxygen (DO) must be high for aquatic life. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) shows organic pollution: high BOD means low DO. COD (chemical oxygen demand) includes chemically oxidisable matter and is higher than BOD. Eutrophication from nutrients causes algal bloom and fish kills. India’s biggest source is untreated sewage. CPCB's criteria for bathing water ask for DO of 5 mg/l or more and BOD of 3 mg/l or less. Other indicators are the faecal coliform count, which shows sewage contamination, plus pH, turbidity and total dissolved solids. Bioindicators help too: some insect larvae such as stoneflies live only in clean water, while sludge worms survive in polluted water.
Natural and man-made problems

Fluoride above 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis (Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh). Arsenic above 0.01 mg/L causes skin and cancer problems (Ganga plains, West Bengal, Bihar). Nitrate rises from fertiliser. Over-extraction also draws up salt and uranium in some areas. The Central Ground Water Board monitors this. Fluorosis damages teeth and bones, and arsenic exposure also causes skin lesions. The WHO guideline value for arsenic is 0.01 mg per litre, which India's drinking water standard follows. Over-extraction is highest in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, where the water table falls every year. Rainwater harvesting, managed aquifer recharge and the Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) address this.
What exists

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 set up the CPCB and State Boards. The Water Cess Act 1977 taxes water use. Jan Vishwas amendments (2023–24) replaced many jail terms with penalties. The Ganga Action Plan began in 1985. Namami Gange (2014) is run by the National Mission for Clean Ganga with sewage treatment as its core. The Ganga became a National River in 2008. Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) aims at tap water in every rural home. Under the 1974 Act, no one may discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream without the State Board's consent. It was India's first modern pollution law. Under the Environment Protection Act 1986 the Centre sets effluent standards. Practical tools are sewage treatment plants (STPs), common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) and zero liquid discharge norms. Namami Gange also covers industrial effluent monitoring and riverfront development.
Quiet and slow

Causes: excess pesticide and fertiliser, industrial effluent, mining, solid waste, irrigation with polluted water. Result: salinity, alkalinity, loss of microbes, heavy metals entering food. The Soil Health Card scheme (2015) promotes balanced use. Organic farming schemes such as PKVY reduce chemical load. Contaminated site rules remain weak in India.
Rules and limits

Noise is measured in decibels (dB). The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 under the EPA give day (6 am to 10 pm) and night limits. Day/night limits in dB(A): industrial 75/70, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, silence zone 50/40. Silence zones extend to 100 m around hospitals, schools and courts. Loudspeakers are restricted between 10 pm and 6 am with limited exceptions.
Thermal and marine

Thermal pollution comes from power plant coolant water. It lowers oxygen in rivers. Oil spills harm seabirds and coasts. The MARPOL convention (1973/78) regulates ship pollution. Plastic and microplastics now reach even the Himalaya and the deep sea. Thermal pollution also changes breeding and kills heat-sensitive fish because warm water holds less dissolved oxygen. Oil spills are cleaned with booms, skimmers and dispersants, and the Indian Coast Guard handles response under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan. Microplastics are particles under five millimetres and enter food chains through fish and salt.
Law is strong, enforcement is weak

State Pollution Control Boards are short of staff and funds, and sometimes politically pressured. Decriminalisation (Jan Vishwas) is defended as ease of doing business but criticised as weakening deterrence. The polluter pays principle is accepted, yet recovery of environmental compensation is slow. River cleaning has focused on building plants; poor running and no ecological flow remain problems. NGT orders and court-imposed environmental compensation have forced some cleanups, yet many orders go unmet. Audits have pointed to unspent funds and delays in river projects. Experts propose independent monitoring, real-time online emission monitoring, a larger role for communities, and treating wastewater as a resource for reuse in industry and farming.
Rivers and cases

The Yamuna in Delhi, the Ganga near Kanpur and the Adyar and Cooum in Chennai are standard examples. The NGT has monitored Ganga and Yamuna cleaning. The Supreme Court’s M.C. Mehta v Union of India (Ganga tanneries) and the Vellore Citizens case (1996) established the precautionary principle and polluter pays.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Despite crores spent, Indian rivers remain polluted. Why? Suggest reforms.” Structure: causes (sewage gap, industry, agriculture); programmes (GAP, Namami Gange); failures (design, running costs, ecological flow, governance); way forward (decentralised treatment, reuse, river basin authorities). Prelims tip: BOD high means worse water. Fluoride limit 1.5 mg/L. Silence zone 100 m. Water Act 1974.
Solid, Plastic, E-waste and Hazardous Waste
Waste is a governance test

India generates tens of millions of tonnes of solid waste a year, and city dumps like Ghazipur in Delhi are visible failures. UPSC asks about the rule sets, the EPR idea and global treaties. Learn each rule with its year. Mains likes the idea that waste is a resource problem, not just a disposal problem.
The waste hierarchy

Reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Landfill is the last option. A circular economy keeps materials in use. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes the maker of a product responsible for its waste after use. It is the main tool in Indian rules for plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres.
Solid Waste Management Rules 2016

The 2016 rules replaced the 2000 rules. They require source segregation into wet, dry and domestic hazardous waste, extend to areas beyond municipal limits, bring in bulk waste generators , and push composting and waste-to-energy. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 , notified in January 2026 and in force from 1 April 2026, replaced the 2016 rules. They require segregation into four streams: wet, dry, sanitary and special care waste. Related: Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 aims at garbage-free cities. Indore is the model city.
Rules and bans

The Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 were amended in 2021. Identified single-use plastics were banned from 1 July 2022. Carry bag thickness was raised to 75 microns (September 2021) and 120 microns (December 2022). The 2022 EPR guidelines for plastic packaging set recycling targets and mandate registration on a central portal. Plastic credits can be traded.
E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022

India is among the largest producers of e-waste. The 2022 rules (in force April 2023) replaced the 2016 rules. They set EPR targets and certificates for producers, and cover refurbishers and recyclers. Informal recyclers handle most e-waste, exposing workers to lead, mercury and burning fumes. Linking them to formal channels is a major Mains point.
The family of rules

Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 : includes control of cross-border movement. Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016 with colour-coded bags. Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016 . Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 with EPR. Basel Convention (1989) bans dumping of hazardous waste in poorer countries; Rotterdam (1998) is prior informed consent; Stockholm (2001) targets persistent organic pollutants.
The treaty talks

The UN agreed in 2022 to negotiate a legally binding plastics treaty. Talks in Busan (December 2024) and Geneva (August 2025) ended without agreement, split over production caps versus waste management. India’s stance favours waste management and common but differentiated responsibilities, and resists production caps.
EPR and the informal sector

EPR can fund recycling, but credits may be traded on paper without real collection. Critics say the rules ignore the role of waste pickers, who are the real recyclers. Waste-to-energy plants also face criticism for low-calorific mixed waste, air emissions and costs. Source segregation, not technology, is the weak link.
Cities and legacy dumps

Landfill fires and trash mountains at Ghazipur, Bhalswa and Deonar are recurring news. Programmes such as Swachh Bharat and bio-mining of legacy waste try to clear them. Indore, Surat and Ambikapur show that segregation and community systems work. Kerala’s Haritha Karma Sena uses women’s groups.
How to answer

Mains-style: “E-waste is an emerging threat. Examine India’s regulatory framework and gaps.” Structure: scale; rules (2016 then 2022 EPR); implementation gaps (informal sector, low collection); way forward (formalisation, design for repair, right to repair). Mains-style: “Discuss EPR as a tool for plastic waste management.” Prelims tip: Learn each year: SWM 2016, Plastic 2016 (amended 2021), E-waste 2022, Battery 2022. Basel = hazardous waste.
Deforestation, Desertification and Land Degradation
Land is a climate and livelihood issue

Nearly 30 percent of India’s land is degraded. UPSC links this to food security, floods, migration and climate. The key laws and conventions (UNCCD, Forest Conservation Act, FRA) appear in Prelims and Mains. The core idea is Land Degradation Neutrality : no net loss of healthy land.
Three linked terms

Deforestation is clearing forest for other uses. Land degradation is loss of productivity from erosion, salinity, waterlogging or loss of vegetation. Desertification is degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas from climate and human activity. It does not mean desert spreading by sand alone. Water erosion is the largest cause of degradation in India, followed by vegetation loss and wind erosion.
Why it happens

Agriculture expansion, shifting cultivation (jhum) with short fallows. Mining, dams and roads; urban sprawl. Overgrazing and fuelwood collection. Unsustainable irrigation causing salinity and waterlogging, for example in Punjab and Haryana. Climate change: drought and extreme rain.
India’s land

The SAC-ISRO Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas reported that about 97.85 million hectares (nearly 29.7 percent of India’s area) was degraded in 2018–19. The main hotspots are Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat and Delhi. India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030 under the Bonn Challenge and the UNCCD, and to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent. The atlas shows water erosion as the largest single process of degradation, followed by vegetation degradation and wind erosion. Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas; the Thar is the main arid region, and the Aravalli range has also lost cover. Degradation lowers soil carbon, water-holding capacity and crop yield.
The global treaty

The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994 (Paris) and entered into force in 1996. It is a result of the 1992 Rio Summit and is the only legally binding convention on land. It has a bottom-up approach with national action programmes. India hosted UNCCD COP14 in Greater Noida in 2019. The Delhi Declaration stressed land restoration and gender. Other efforts: the Bonn Challenge (2011), Africa’s Great Green Wall , and India’s plan for an Aravalli green belt.
Forest Conservation Act and the 2023 change

The Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 bars diversion of forest land without Central approval. In 1996 the T.N. Godavarman case widened the meaning of forest to its dictionary sense. The 2023 amendment (renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam) limits the Act to land notified as forest or recorded as forest after 25 October 1980. It exempts some linear projects near borders and security infrastructure up to set sizes. The Supreme Court has directed that the wider 1996 definition be applied for now (as of 2024).
Rights and money

The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights for Scheduled Tribes and other traditional dwellers. CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act 2016) pays for afforestation when forest land is diverted. Joint Forest Management (1990) involves village committees. Green India Mission is under the NAPCC. The campaign “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” (2024) encourages tree planting.
Compensatory afforestation is not equal

Critics say planting trees elsewhere does not replace a natural forest. Plantations store less biodiversity and are often on poor land. Funds sit unspent for years. Development needs, such as the Great Nicobar project and coal mining in Hasdeo Arand, create a standing conflict between growth and forest.
Examples

Ravines of the Chambal, salinity in the Indo-Gangetic canal belt, and loss of mangroves in the Sundarbans are land degradation cases. Rajasthan’s Thar is spreading at the edges. Sikkim and Mizoram show better forest outcomes with community control. Meghalaya and Nagaland have community forests. The Chambal ravines were formed by gully erosion of soft alluvium. Canal irrigation without drainage causes waterlogging and salinity in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. In the Sundarbans, rising seas, cyclones and shrimp farming damage mangroves. Community forest management, such as Joint Forest Management and Van Panchayats in Uttarakhand, shows that local control can improve forest condition.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is land degradation? How does it affect food security, and what steps has India taken?” Structure: definition; extent (nearly 30 percent); causes; effects on yield and livelihoods; policy (soil health card, watershed development, Bonn commitment, UNCCD); way forward. Mains-style: “Critically evaluate the 2023 Forest Conservation amendment.” Prelims tip: UNCCD 1994, entered into force 1996, COP14 in India 2019. Bonn Challenge 2011. Prelims tip: the World Day to Combat Desertification is 17 June. The Forest Survey of India publishes the India State of Forest Report every two years. In answers use data from the atlas and name schemes: Soil Health Card (2015), watershed development under PMKSY, the Green India Mission and CAMPA funds. End with land degradation neutrality, which is SDG target 15.3.
Wetlands, Mangroves and Coral Reefs
Coastal and wetland ecosystems are Prelims gold

Ramsar sites, Montreux Record, mangroves and coral bleaching appear in nearly every Prelims. Mains asks about coastal regulation and blue carbon. These ecosystems protect coasts, store carbon and feed millions. They are also among the most threatened. These ecosystems sit at the boundary of land and water. Wetlands hold flood water, mangroves slow storm surge, and coral reefs break waves. They also store large amounts of carbon, called blue carbon, in plants and mud. Link each ecosystem to its law or scheme and a named site; examples such as Chilika, Sundarbans and Lakshadweep appear often.
Definition and Ramsar

The Ramsar Convention (Iran, 1971; in force 1975) is the global treaty for wetlands. It promotes wise use . Sites are listed under the Ramsar List. The Montreux Record lists sites with damaged ecology. In India it includes Keoladeo and Loktak. World Wetlands Day is 2 February. India’s Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017 replaced the 2010 rules and set a State Wetland Authority. Ramsar defines wetlands broadly: marshes, fens, peatlands, lakes, rivers, mangroves, coral reefs, and even paddy fields, plus marine water up to six metres deep at low tide. Wetlands filter water, recharge groundwater, store floodwater and support birds and fish. The Convention rests on three pillars: wise use, listing of sites, and international cooperation.
As of 2026

India’s first Ramsar sites were Chilika and Keoladeo (1981). As of 2026, India has about 100 Ramsar sites (reports during the year range from 98 to 103), the most in Asia. India ranks first in Asia and third in the world by number. Tamil Nadu has the most sites. The Sundarbans is the largest Ramsar site in India by area.
Salt-loving forests

Mangroves grow in the intertidal zone. Adaptations: pneumatophores (breathing roots), stilt roots , viviparity (seeds germinate on the tree) and salt excretion. They guard against cyclones and tsunamis, nurse fish and store “blue carbon.” India has roughly 5,000 sq km of mangroves (ISFR). West Bengal (Sundarbans) has the biggest share, followed by Gujarat and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Policy

Budget 2023–24 announced MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes) and Amrit Dharohar for wetlands. Mangroves are protected in CRZ-I under the Coastal Regulation Zone rules. The Green Credit Programme also lists mangrove restoration as an activity. MISHTI aims to restore mangroves along the coast and the salt pans, using convergence with MGNREGS and CAMPA funds. Amrit Dharohar encourages the wise use of wetlands and aims to boost bird tourism and local incomes. Under CRZ rules, the zones range from CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive) to CRZ-IV (waters), and the 2019 notification set no-development zones near the shore.
Living limestone

Corals are animals (polyps) with algae called zooxanthellae living inside them. They give colour and food. Reefs are fringing , barrier or atoll . They need warm (about 23 to 29 °C), clear, shallow, saline water. They cover under 1 percent of the ocean but support about a quarter of marine species. Corals build a calcium carbonate skeleton, and reefs form over thousands of years. In India reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Reef algae need light, so reefs stay in shallow water and avoid muddy river mouths. Reefs protect coasts from waves and support fisheries and tourism.
Threat

When water is too warm, corals expel algae and turn white: bleaching . Other threats: ocean acidification, pollution, dynamite fishing and cyclones. The world has seen a fourth global bleaching event since 2023, the most widespread on record. India’s reef regions are the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
CRZ Notification 2019

The Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019 replaced the 2011 rules. CRZ-I is ecologically sensitive (mangroves, corals; with an inter-tidal part), CRZ-II is built-up urban shore, CRZ-III is rural and undeveloped, and CRZ-IV covers water area up to 12 nautical miles. Critics argue the 2019 rules allowed more building near beaches. Supporters say they help livelihoods and give clearer zones.
Examples

Chilika (Odisha), Loktak (Manipur), Sundarbans , Bhitarkanika mangroves and Gulf of Mannar corals are key cases. Kolkata’s East Kolkata Wetlands treat the city’s sewage naturally. Wetlands are lost to reclamation and encroachment in Bengaluru, Chennai and Srinagar, and floods in Chennai (2015) showed the cost.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Why are wetlands called the kidneys of the landscape? What threats do Indian wetlands face?” Structure: functions; Ramsar and rules; threats (encroachment, sewage, invasives); remedies (wise use, community role, Amrit Dharohar). Prelims tip: Montreux Record: Keoladeo and Loktak. First Ramsar sites: Chilika and Keoladeo. Mangroves are CRZ-I. Know the five reef areas.
Climate Change: Science and the Greenhouse Effect
The spine of the syllabus

Climate change links to agriculture, water, energy, security and diplomacy. UPSC asks the science in Prelims and the policy in Mains. A sound base here makes the next eight lessons easy. Always use the latest numbers and date them. The topic also connects with geography, such as the monsoon and glaciers, and with economy through energy and agriculture. UPSC asks the basic science, such as the gases, global warming potential and feedbacks, in Prelims. Mains asks for India's position, adaptation and finance. Use IPCC reports as the standard source for evidence, and give the year.
The natural greenhouse effect

Sunlight warms Earth. Earth sends heat back as long-wave radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb some of it and re-emit it, keeping the planet about 33 °C warmer than it would be. This is natural and needed for life. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect : humans have added gases since the industrial era. Greenhouse gases are transparent to incoming short-wave sunlight but absorb outgoing long-wave infrared. Without them the average surface temperature would be about minus 18 °C instead of about 15 °C. Water vapour is the strongest natural greenhouse gas, but its amount responds to temperature, so it acts as a feedback rather than a driver. Venus shows a runaway case of the effect.
GWP and the Kyoto six

The six Kyoto gases are CO2, methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), HFCs, PFCs and SF6. Global warming potential (GWP) compares them with CO2 (GWP 1). Methane is about 28 times over 100 years but lasts only about a decade. N2O is about 270 times. SF6 is over 23,000 times. Water vapour is the biggest natural greenhouse gas but responds to temperature rather than driving it. Black carbon is a short-lived warming agent, not a gas.
The numbers

The IPCC (set up in 1988 by WMO and UNEP) reported in its Sixth Assessment (2021–23) that human activity has warmed the planet by about 1.1 °C above 1850–1900 levels. CO2 now stands above 420 ppm versus about 280 before industry (as of 2025). The World Meteorological Organization said 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5 °C. A single year above 1.5 °C is not the same as the Paris long-term target, which is measured over decades. Sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018.
Why warming can speed up

Ice-albedo feedback : melting ice exposes dark sea or land, which absorbs more heat. Permafrost thaw releases methane. Warmer oceans hold less CO2. These loops can push the climate past tipping points such as ice-sheet collapse or Amazon dieback. Ocean acidification is a related effect: dissolved CO2 lowers pH and harms corals and shellfish.
El Niño, La Niña, IOD

El Niño warms the eastern Pacific and usually weakens the Indian monsoon. La Niña is the cool phase and usually helps it. The Indian Ocean Dipole can offset El Niño when positive. These cycles cause year-to-year swings; climate change is the long-term trend. India’s monsoon forecasts depend on these links.
Responsibility

China, the US and India are the top three emitters in recent years in absolute terms. India’s per capita emissions are about half the world average, and its cumulative share is small (under 5 percent). This is the basis of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR-RC): historic emitters should lead.
Mitigation or adaptation, and who pays

Developed countries stress cutting emissions everywhere. Developing countries stress adaptation, finance and the right to develop. Some scientists urge carbon removal and geoengineering; others warn of moral hazard. The carbon budget idea gives a fixed amount of CO2 left for a temperature target. Fair shares are the core of the dispute.
India’s position

India is highly exposed to heat, floods, monsoon swings and sea-level rise. It has set a net-zero target for 2070 and stresses equity and climate justice. India is not part of the Global Methane Pledge (2021, 30 percent cut by 2030), citing livestock and rice methane tied to livelihoods.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Explain the greenhouse effect and the evidence for human-induced climate change. Why is India vulnerable?” Structure: mechanism; gases and GWP; IPCC numbers (dated); India’s exposure; two responses. Prelims tip: Kyoto has six gases. Methane has higher GWP but shorter life than CO2. IPCC founded 1988. El Niño usually weakens the monsoon.
Impacts on India: Agriculture, Water, Coasts
India feels climate change first

With 1.4 billion people, a long coast, Himalayan glaciers and a monsoon economy, India is very exposed. UPSC Mains asks for impacts and adaptation in agriculture, water and cities. Use named events and dates in answers. India ranks among the countries most affected in global climate risk indices published by German think tanks. The impacts are linked: a hotter Himalaya and altered monsoon change river flow, which affects farms, power and cities downstream. In answers, use one event per sector, such as the 2022 heatwave for agriculture and the Kerala floods of 2018 for disasters.
Rising extremes

Heatwaves are longer and earlier. In March 2022 an early heatwave cut wheat yields in parts of the north. Cities add the heat-island effect. India’s heat action plans began with Ahmedabad in 2013. Heat also hits outdoor workers and productivity, and raises power demand. Wet-bulb temperature, which combines heat and humidity, is the real danger for people, because the body cannot cool itself by sweating when it is high. The Ahmedabad plan added early warning, cool roofs and public awareness, and the NDMA now guides state and city heat action plans. Outdoor workers, the elderly and the urban poor are most exposed.
Yield and monsoon risk

Agriculture is mostly rain-fed, so changes in the monsoon matter. Heat at grain filling cuts wheat yield. Warmer nights hurt rice. Extreme rain damages standing crops. Pests and diseases shift range. ICAR’s NICRA project studies resilient crops and the ICAR has released many climate-resilient varieties. Insurance (PMFBY) cushions losses. Rain-fed farming covers roughly half of India's net sown area, and its yields swing with the monsoon. Rising sea level and salinity threaten delta rice areas. Shifting sowing dates, drought-tolerant seeds, micro-irrigation and crop diversification are the main adaptations. Warmer winters also shorten the wheat season in the Indo-Gangetic plain.
Glaciers and monsoon

Himalayan glaciers feed the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. They are retreating, first adding flows and later reducing them. Glacial lake outburst floods are a growing hazard: Kedarnath 2013, Chamoli 2021 and South Lhonak, Sikkim in October 2023. Rainfall is becoming more extreme: fewer rainy days but heavier spells. Groundwater is already overused in the north-west.
Sea level and cyclones

India has about 7,500 km of coastline. Rising seas threaten the Sundarbans, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and the Lakshadweep. Salt water enters river deltas and aquifers. Cyclones in the Arabian Sea have grown more intense. Early warning and shelters have cut deaths sharply, as in Odisha after the 1999 super cyclone. Mangroves and coral reefs are natural defences.
Urban floods and landslides

Mumbai (2005), Chennai (2015), Kerala (2018) and Wayanad landslides (2024) show rising flood and slope risk, made worse by poor drainage, wetland loss and building on hills. Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand have faced repeated cloudbursts. The Himalaya’s fragile slopes are an adaptation priority. Urban flooding is driven by concrete cover, choked drains and building on floodplains and wetlands. Chennai's 2015 floods hit areas built over lakes and marshes. Cloudbursts are sudden heavy rain over a small area, which trigger flash floods in hill states. Sponge city ideas, restored wetlands and early warning systems reduce the risk.
Wider effects

Climate change spreads vector-borne diseases, reduces labour hours and worsens food prices. It drives migration from the Sundarbans and drought belts, and stress on shared rivers adds to regional tension. The poor, women and small farmers are hit hardest. This is the equity argument India makes abroad. The IPCC's sixth assessment (2021 to 2023) flagged South Asia as highly vulnerable. Sea-level rise and cyclones put Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai at risk, and climate migration adds pressure on cities. Adaptation, insurance and social protection are needed along with emission cuts.
Adaptation versus mitigation

India’s emissions are low per person, so it argues for adaptation finance. Yet adaptation needs huge money: early warning, resilient crops, drainage and housing. Critics say too much policy is about mitigation targets while state adaptation plans lack funds and data. Adaptation is local: it means drainage in cities, resilient seeds in villages and shelters on the coast. Mitigation is global, because greenhouse gases mix in the air. Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are expected to balance finance between both, yet most climate finance has gone to mitigation. This makes the adaptation gap a key Mains point.
Policy tools

The NAPCC (2008) has missions on agriculture, water, Himalaya and habitat. States have State Action Plans . The NDMA handles disasters under the Disaster Management Act 2005. The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019) was launched by India. The National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change gives limited money. India submitted its updated NDC in 2026 with adaptation themes (see lesson on NDCs). Adaptation is funded mostly by state and national budgets. The Disaster Management Act 2005 sets up the NDMA nationally and State Disaster Management Authorities in states, and the National Disaster Response Force handles response. Early cyclone warnings from the IMD have cut deaths sharply, as in Cyclone Phailin in Odisha in 2013.
How to answer

Mains-style: “How is climate change affecting Indian agriculture? Suggest adaptation measures.” Structure: heat, water and monsoon; crop examples (wheat 2022); regional pattern; adaptation (resilient seeds, micro-irrigation, insurance, crop advisories); finance and extension gaps. Mains-style: “Glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalaya: causes and mitigation.” Prelims tip: GLOF events: Kedarnath 2013, Chamoli 2021, South Lhonak 2023. CDRI launched by India in 2019.
UNFCCC, Kyoto and the Paris Agreement
Treaty facts are Prelims and Mains staples

UPSC asks for the year, the principle and the difference between Kyoto and Paris. Mains asks if the system is fair and working. Master the timeline and the three principles: CBDR-RC, precaution, sustainable development.
The framework, 1992

Adopted at the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and in force from 21 March 1994 . Nearly all countries (about 198 parties) have joined. It states the goal of stabilising greenhouse gases at a safe level. The COP is its supreme body and meets yearly. Annex I lists developed countries and economies in transition. Annex II lists rich countries that must give finance and technology. Others are non-Annex I , including India and China.
Top-down targets

Adopted in 1997 , in force 2005 . Only Annex I countries had legally binding targets: about 5 percent below 1990 levels in the first period (2008–12). The Doha Amendment (2012) set a second period for 2013–20. Flexible tools: emissions trading , Joint Implementation and the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM). The US never ratified; Canada withdrew in 2011. Kyoto covered a shrinking share of global emissions.
Steps in between

Bali Action Plan (2007). Copenhagen (2009): the $100 billion a year pledge and the 2 °C goal, but not binding. Cancun (2010): Green Climate Fund created. Durban (2011): talks for a new universal deal. Lima (2014): intended nationally determined contributions (INDCs). After Kyoto, talks stalled on who should cut emissions. The Bali Action Plan opened a two-track negotiation, and Copenhagen was seen as a failure because the accord was only noted. Cancun brought its pledges into the UN process, including the Green Climate Fund. Durban started the platform that led to Paris, and Lima asked every country to submit its contribution before Paris.
Adopted 2015

Adopted on 12 December 2015 at COP21 and in force on 4 November 2016 . It is universal and legally binding on process, not on targets. Goal: keep warming well below 2 °C , pursue 1.5 °C , reach peak and then balance of sources and sinks in the second half of the century, and align finance. Each country sets its own Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and renews it every five years with a ratchet (no backsliding). Unlike Kyoto's top-down targets, Paris is bottom-up. Its transparency framework requires countries to report emissions and progress. A global stocktake happens every five years, and the first was completed at COP28 in 2023. Article 6 covers carbon markets, Article 8 recognises loss and damage, and Article 9 sets finance duties, with developed countries asked to lead.
Key articles

Article 6 : carbon markets and cooperative approaches. Rules were finalised at COP29 (Baku, 2024). Article 7 : global goal on adaptation. Article 8 : loss and damage. Article 9 : finance from developed countries. Article 13 : enhanced transparency framework. Article 14 : Global Stocktake every five years. The first ended at COP28 (2023).
Rulebook and review

The Katowice rulebook (COP24, 2018) set the detailed rules. COP26 Glasgow (2021) asked countries to revisit targets and agreed to phase down unabated coal. The Global Stocktake concluded at COP28 (Dubai, 2023) and called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems. By 2025 countries were due to submit new NDCs for 2035. Many were late, and India filed its updated NDC in 2026.
Kyoto versus Paris

Kyoto was top-down, binding for rich countries only, but limited in reach. Paris is bottom-up and universal, but targets are voluntary and current pledges still point beyond 2 °C without more action. The US formally left Paris with effect from January 2026 (second time), which weakens finance. Developing countries say CBDR-RC has been diluted.
India’s stand

India ratified Paris in October 2016. It insists on equity, CBDR-RC, a historic responsibility link, climate finance and technology transfer. It supports market mechanisms with safeguards and opposes unilateral carbon border taxes such as the EU’s CBAM. India’s net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 (2021).
How to answer

Mains-style: “Compare the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. Which is better for India?” Structure: Kyoto top-down, only Annex I; Paris bottom-up, NDCs; equity and finance; India’s gains (flexibility, space to develop) and risks (pressure to raise targets, CBAM). Mains-style: “CBDR-RC: is it being diluted?” Prelims tip: UNFCCC adopted 1992, in force 1994. Kyoto adopted 1997, in force 2005. Paris adopted 2015, in force 2016. CDM is under Kyoto’s Article 12.
COPs and Climate Finance
COP outcomes are the most current part of the paper

UPSC asks about the latest COP, the finance goal and India’s position. These answers must carry names, numbers and years. As of 2026: COP30 (Belém, Brazil) ended in November 2025. COP31 is due in Antalya, Türkiye in November 2026 as this lesson is written, so check its outcome.
What a COP is

The Conference of the Parties is the supreme body of the UNFCCC. It meets every year. A Presidency (host country) steers talks, and decisions are by consensus. The Subsidiary Bodies (SBSTA, SBI) prepare technical work. Alongside it, the CMA governs the Paris Agreement. The COP presidency rotates among the five UN regional groups. Decisions need consensus, which means that a single objecting party can slow talks. Observers include NGOs and business groups. The UNFCCC secretariat is in Bonn, and the first COP was held in Berlin in 1995. COP3 produced the Kyoto Protocol in 1997, and COP21 in Paris produced the Paris Agreement.
Dubai 2023 and Baku 2024

COP28 (Dubai): the first Global Stocktake called for transitioning away from fossil fuels , tripling renewable capacity to 11,000 GW and doubling efficiency by 2030. The Loss and Damage Fund was launched on day one. COP29 (Baku): the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) set $300 billion a year by 2035 from developed countries, within a wider aim of $1.3 trillion a year from all sources. India called the offer inadequate. Article 6 carbon market rules were also settled. Dubai gave direction and Baku gave money. The stocktake judged that countries were off track for the 1.5 °C goal. The Loss and Damage Fund is hosted by the World Bank as an interim arrangement. At Baku, developing countries said the finance sum was far below need, and India objected at the closing plenary.
Belém 2025

COP30 was held in Belém, Brazil, in the Amazon. It ended with the Global Mutirão decision. Main results: a call to triple adaptation finance by 2035 (without a clear base year), voluntary Belém adaptation indicators , a Just Transition mechanism, a two-year work programme on climate finance and a push to speed up implementation. The text did not name a roadmap to end fossil fuels, and deforestation had no roadmap in the final text. Brazil promised to prepare voluntary roadmaps. The Tropical Forests Forever Facility was launched with pledges from some countries.
Positions

India stressed equity, CBDR-RC and finance, and opposed unilateral trade measures like the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) , whose definitive phase began in January 2026. It supported adaptation finance and a just transition. India argued that developed countries must deliver the earlier $100 billion promise and scale it up before asking developing countries to do more.
Antalya 2026

Türkiye will host COP31 in Antalya in November 2026. Under a compromise, Australia leads the negotiations as President of the negotiations, and a pre-COP in the Pacific is planned (as of 2026, reports; verify final arrangements). Watch for the 2035 NDC gap, the finance work programme, adaptation indicators and the fossil fuel roadmap.
The architecture

Global Environment Facility (1991): finances UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD work. Green Climate Fund (Cancun 2010, Songdo, South Korea): the largest dedicated fund. Adaptation Fund (under Kyoto). Loss and Damage Fund (operational from COP28; hosted by the World Bank). LDCF and SCCF for least developed countries.
Delivery

Copenhagen (2009) promised $100 billion a year by 2020. The OECD reported it was first met in 2022. Developing countries dispute how loans are counted and how much is grant. The NCQG replaces it from 2025, but the $300 billion figure is far below the $1.3 trillion need, and much will be loans.
Mitigation versus adaptation finance

Most money goes to mitigation, such as solar. Adaptation gets less and loss and damage the least. Climate finance is also seen as debt creation for poor countries. Rich countries say public money is limited and private capital must be mobilised. Developing countries want public grants.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Climate finance is the real test of Paris. Examine the gaps and India’s position.” Structure: needs; promise ($100 billion, NCQG $300 billion); gaps (loans, accounting, adaptation); India’s demand (grants, CBDR, no CBAM); way forward (reform of MDBs, Article 6, carbon markets). Prelims tip: GCF from Cancun 2010, HQ in Songdo. NCQG is $300 billion by 2035. COP28 Dubai started the Loss and Damage Fund.
Ozone, Montreal Protocol and Other Conventions
Convention names and years are free marks

Prelims often matches a convention with its subject or year. The Montreal Protocol is also the most cited success story in global environmental governance. Learn the ozone chain, then the table of conventions. Prelims often tests pairs such as Basel with hazardous waste, Ramsar with wetlands, and Minamata with mercury. Build a timeline in your head: 1971 Ramsar, 1972 Stockholm and World Heritage, 1973 CITES, 1987 Montreal, 1992 Rio. Also remember that Vienna is the framework and Montreal is the protocol with binding limits.
What and where

Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere (peak about 20 to 30 km up) absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C. It is measured in Dobson Units . Ground-level ozone is a pollutant. Rowland and Molina (1974) warned about CFCs. In 1985 Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin reported the Antarctic ozone hole. Crutzen, Rowland and Molina won the Nobel Prize in 1995. UV-B can cause skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and plankton. The ozone hole forms over Antarctica each spring (September to October) because polar stratospheric clouds help chlorine destroy ozone. Remember the contrast: stratospheric ozone is protective, while tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a pollutant.
Chlorine chain

CFCs are stable, drift up, and in the stratosphere UV frees chlorine. One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. The hole forms in the Antarctic spring (September to October) because polar stratospheric clouds help the reaction. Other ozone depleting substances (ODS): halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, methyl bromide, HCFCs.
The treaties

The Vienna Convention (1985) set up cooperation. The Montreal Protocol (1987, in force 1989) phases out ODS. It is the first treaty ratified by every country in the world. It works with a Multilateral Fund to help developing countries, and has binding timetables. Amendments: London (1990), Copenhagen (1992), Montreal (1997), Beijing (1999) and Kigali (2016) .
HFCs

HFCs do not harm ozone but are strong greenhouse gases. The Kigali Amendment (in force 2019) phases them down. India ratified it in 2021. India’s schedule: freeze in 2028 and cuts in steps, with an 85 percent reduction by 2047, later than developed countries. Scientists project the ozone layer recovering by about 2040 (most of the world), 2045 (Arctic) and 2066 (Antarctic), per UNEP’s 2022 assessment.
Biodiversity and land

Ramsar 1971: wetlands. World Heritage Convention 1972. CITES 1973: trade in endangered species. CMS 1979 (Bonn): migratory species. CBD 1992 with Cartagena Protocol (2000, biosafety) and Nagoya Protocol (2010, access and benefit sharing). UNCCD 1994: desertification. The Ramsar and World Heritage conventions protect sites, while CITES and CMS protect species. CBD, adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has three goals: conservation, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits. Its Kunming-Montreal framework of 2022 sets global biodiversity goals. UNCCD, also born at Rio, is the only legally binding convention on land.
Chemicals and seas

Basel 1989: hazardous waste. Rotterdam 1998: prior informed consent for chemicals. Stockholm 2001: persistent organic pollutants. Minamata 2013: mercury (in force 2017). MARPOL 1973/78: ship pollution. BBNJ (High Seas Treaty), adopted 2023 and in force from January 2026. The Basel Convention covers cross-border movement of hazardous waste.
